title: Stress corpus runbook: quantization vs SLA tradeoffs
content:
Objective:
This is a lightweight runbook and experiment log for a stress-corpus driven investigation into quantization performance vs SLA/quality tradeoffs. We want a repeatable matrix that stresses kernels, KV caching, and routing so we can find breakpoints where cost-optimized quantized variants (INT8 / AWQ / GPTQ) start violating latency SLOs or introduce unacceptable quality regressions.

Background / motivation:
- Many teammates have run microbenchmarks; this exercise targets realistic multi-tenant shaped traffic (short chat bursts + long-context completions) to expose worst-path behaviors not visible in single-profile sweeps.
- Focus: where to place conservative vs aggressive routing defaults and automated fallback thresholds for production.

Stress corpus description (how we generate load):
- Mix: 60% short chat (avg seq 64, median 48), 30% medium (seq 256), 10% long-context (seq 1024+ with KV warmups).
- Client mix: 40% low-concurrency steady clients, 60% bursty clients with spikes (bursts up to 200 concurrent reqs for 10s every 2 min).
- Input patterns: random prefix diversity + content-heavy prompts to exercise attention layers and KV cache touches.
- Repeatable seed set: stress_corpus_v1 (check linked_artifacts in PR)

Test matrix (high level):
- Models: small-medium open models used by product (approx 7B-13B footprints).
- Quant variants: FP16 baseline, INT8 (symmetric asymmetric as applicable), FP8 experimental, GPTQ, AWQ.
- Kernel backends: default optimized GEMM, tensorcore-tuned, custom-quant-kernel-v2 (PR 3421), fallback scalar path.
- Hardware: A100-80GB, H100 (profile both where available).
- Routing configs: always-quant, dynamic-routing-with-fallback, mixed-pool (one pool quant, one pool fp16).
- Concurrency shapes: steady 50 qps, burst 500 qps; per-worker batch windows: 2ms, 8ms, 20ms.

Instrumentation / metrics collected:
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 for token generation and request end-to-end.
- Throughput: tokens/sec absolute and per-GPU.
- Cost proxy: avg tokens per second * GPU cost model (simple).
- Quality signals: perplexity on held-out completion set, token-level edit distance on curated evals, small set of human-readable prompt regressions (5 prompt probes).
- Kernel-level: kernel run time breakdown, memory bandwidth utilization, warp divergence counters (where supported), L2 miss rates, kernel queue times.

Summary of runs (notes):
- Run A: FP16 baseline, steady 50 qps on A100. All good: p95 ~ 120ms for short seq, p99 ~ 230ms.
- Run B: INT8 symmetric aggressive, same traffic. Observed p95 increases by 10–25ms on short chat; p99 tail widened to 350ms for bursts. Kernel traces show occasional kernel retry path causing 1–2ms spikes per call but those aggregated under bursts.
- Run C: AWQ (aggressive packing), tensorcore-kernel, bursty traffic. Throughput improved on medium sequences but long-context heavy requests saw throughput collapse (GPU memory copying spikes). Root cause appears to be KV-cache eviction and rehydration frequency exacerbated by quant kernel memory layout differences.
- Run D: GPTQ with dynamic-routing fallback (if p95 > threshold then route to fp16 pool). This reduced visible quality regressions but introduced 2–4% extra cost due to fallback frequency in burst windows.

Key observations / hypotheses:
- Kernel memory layout for AWQ leads to less predictable L2 access patterns; in long-context workloads this exposes higher L2 misses and DMA stall time, which amplifies latency tail.
- INT8 aggressive variants perform well for throughput but increase kernel fragmentation under high-concurrency multiplexing (batch packing + per-request small batch windows), producing a heavier p99.
- Warm KV cache patterns matter: when clients reuse prefixes the quant kernels show larger latency benefits; with highly diverse prefixes quantized kernels pay a penalty due to repeated KV reconstruction.
- Tensorcore-optimized paths help steady-state throughput but are brittle under mixed sequence-length multiplexing due to less flexible tiling strategies.

Immediate mitigations tried:
- Prefix-aware routing: identify high-reuse prefixes and pin to quant pool; dynamic measure produced ~8% tail reduction.
- Batch-window tuning: increasing max batch window from 8ms to 20ms reduced p99 under INT8 by absorbing burstiness at slight p50 cost.
- Memory-layout fallbacks: for long-context requests route to FP16/tensorcore path when sequence length > threshold. This reduced long-context throughput collapse but increased overall GPU cost.

Runbook for new experiments (step-by-step):
1) Checkout PR 3421 and ensure custom-quant-kernel-v2 is installed on test cluster.
2) Start A100 cluster with 4 workers, populate stress_corpus_v1 dataset.
3) Baseline collect: run FP16 baseline 30m. Save traces to /tmp/quant-stress-traces/baseline.
4) Run INT8 symmetric aggressive for 30m. Capture kernel traces + client replay logs.
5) Run AWQ tensorcore for 30m. Pay special attention to long-context slices; flush KV cache between phases to reproduce cold-start patterns.
6) Collect and aggregate: use the profiling pipeline (see linked PR) to produce per-kernel breakdowns and tail-latency overlays.
7) Run permutation with dynamic-routing enabled; compute fallback frequency and cost delta.
8) Archive results and tag experiments with jira ticket JIRA-RT-1173.

What to look for in traces (debug checklist):
- sudden jumps in memcpy/PCIe times -> indicates memory layout misfit / large staging copies
- kernel queue pileups -> scheduler contention (multiple slow kernels blocking fast ones)
- frequent KV rehydration events for same client -> caching policy bug or layout-induced cache thrash
- p99 spikes correlated with specific kernel variants -> consider blacklisting kernel until fix

Open questions / unknowns:
- FP8 behavior on H100: we saw some promising throughput but no stable quantization pipeline yet; need to quantify quality drift on our eval set.
- How does multiworkload multiplexing across different model sizes affect kernel scheduling fairness? Preliminary traces show larger models blocking smaller ones when quantized kernels have longer tails.
- Is there a cheap on-device heuristic to predict when a request will cause KV churn (and therefore should be routed to fp16)?

Action items / next steps:
- (Ethan) instrument L2 miss counters during AWQ runs and attach heatmaps to PR 3421 (due 2026-02-19).
- (Priya) run focused FP8 pilot on H100 with long-context corpus (due 2026-02-22).
- (Maya) prototype prefix-pin heuristic and run A/B to measure tail reduction and fallback frequency (due 2026-02-25).
- Collate results into a short playbook for routing defaults and push to Confluence when stable.

Notes to self:
- Keep this doc lightweight; the canonical artifact will be the notebook in PR 3421 and the confluence runbook. Use this page for quick experiment logs.
- When filing follow-ups, include exact stress_corpus seed and cluster snapshot id to allow repros.

Appendix (quick links):
- PR with kernel changes: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/3421
- Jira ticket tracking experiments: JIRA-RT-1173
- Corpus seed and generator: confluence://Quant-Runbook-2026#stress_corpus_v1

End of runbook entry.
